claim: Name resolution behaves exactly as the four listed rules say: missing/empty name means the reserved `default` profile; a name failing `validate_profile_name` (1-64 chars from `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`) raises `ProfileNameError` before the agent runs; a valid name with no stored profile falls back to the stored `default`; with no stored `default`, every field comes from the base config.
source_excerpt:
- A missing or empty name means the reserved `default` profile.
- A name that is not a valid identifier (1 to 64 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`, checked by `validate_profile_name`) raises `ProfileNameError` before the agent runs.
- A valid name with no stored profile falls back to the stored `default` profile.
- If there is no stored `default` profile, every field comes from the base config.

claim: An `OSError`, invalid JSON, or a non-object top-level value sets `load_error` to a message starting with `Warning:`, logs it, leaves no profiles loaded and leaves the bad file on disk; a single invalid entry is skipped and logged per line, with `load_error` naming every skipped entry when all entry names are valid; an entry whose name fails `validate_profile_name` is skipped, all writes are refused until renamed and restarted, and `load_error` then reports only the count of invalid names.
source_excerpt:
- A file that cannot be read (an `OSError`), invalid JSON, or a top-level value that is not an object sets `load_error` to a message that starts with `Warning:`, logs it, and leaves the store with no profiles. The bad file stays on disk.
- A single entry that fails validation is skipped and logged on its own line. When every entry name is valid, `load_error` names every skipped entry.
- An entry whose name fails `validate_profile_name` is skipped, and all writes are refused until an operator renames it in the file and restarts. This stops a save from deleting the entries that were skipped. In this case `load_error` reports only the count of invalid names. Any entries skipped for a bad body are named only in their per-entry log lines.
verify_hint: Check `_read_from_disk` and the write guard in `src/sqllens/profiles.py`; falsifying inputs are a profiles file whose top level is a JSON list, a file with one bad-body entry plus one bad-name entry, and a write attempted while a bad-name entry is present

claim: The glossary's RefusalRedactingRunner entry now describes only what the runner actually does: it replaces refusal text with the refusal kind, and its logging claim is scoped so the RlsError-with-non-refusal-cause path (whose full reason is logged nowhere) does not contradict it.
verify_against: RefusalRedactingRunner and _logged_by_guard in src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py, and the RlsError raised by traverse_scope failure in src/sqllens/safety/rls.py
verify_hint: Compare the glossary's RefusalRedactingRunner entry with RefusalRedactingRunner/_logged_by_guard in src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py (~lines 960-1016) and rls.py's 'could not analyze SQL scopes' raise
prior_evidence: RefusalRedactingRunner (rule_sets.py:983-1016) catches UnsafeSqlError and RlsError, so it covers every refusal type (RuleSetRefusal, WholeRowSelectError, RlsError), and it logs at WARNING. But the claim says it logs the full reason, and that fails for one path. When a refusal has a non-refusal __cause__, _logged_by_guard (971-980) assumes the guard already logged the cause, and line 1011 then logs only the kind fields (the exception text is dropped). rls.py:265-273 raises RlsError('could not analyze SQL scopes ...: {e}') from e when traverse_scope fails, and rls.py has no logger at all (grep 'logg' finds no match). That RlsError therefore reaches the redactor with a non-refusal cause, gets redacted to REDACTED_RLS, and its full reason is logged nowhere. The docstring at 984 and the glossary claim 'log the full reason at WARNING' for every refusal, so this case contradicts them. Also, RuleSetRefusal is re-raised unchanged (1002-1004) and its reason is logged by RuleSetGuardRunner (880), which is fine. Guard-internal errors get REDACTED_GUARD_ERROR (961), which is not a refusal kind.

claim: The glossary's catalog-check entry describes check_catalog's actual scope: existence checks for every listed table and column, with type comparison limited to the typed entries (compare-rule columns, parent_rule compare columns, owner_via link_user_column), and it does not claim startup-only execution.

prior_evidence: check_catalog (src/sqllens/rule_sets.py:1118-1190) does check that every listed table (BASE TABLE) and column exists, and it runs at startup via preflight.probe_database -> _check_rule_set_catalog (preflight.py:151-154, 166) when a rule-set file is configured on MySQL. But the type check is narrower than the glossary claims: only `typed` entries from _catalog_reads (rules_sets.py:1091-1100) are compared against DATA_TYPE (lines 1178-1186). Those are compare-rule columns, parent_rule compare columns, and owner_via link_user_column. Ordinary listed columns, predicate columns and link row/target columns are checked for existence only, with no type check. The glossary line (docs/internal/glossary.md:11) says every table and column exists 'with the expected type', which overstates this. The check_catalog docstring itself limits type checking to compare columns and link_user_column. The check also runs at request time via ensure_catalog_confirmed, not only at startup, which the glossary does not say.

claim: ci-and-distribution.md's release.yml description matches the workflow's actual job dependency graph, where smoke and github-release both depend on [build, pypi-publish] and therefore run in parallel rather than in a strict four-job sequence.
verify_against: The job ids and `needs:` declarations in .github/workflows/release.yml
verify_hint: Compare the release.yml section of docs/internal/operations/ci-and-distribution.md with the `needs:` lines of the smoke and github-release jobs in .github/workflows/release.yml
prior_evidence: Most details match release.yml: job ids build, pypi-publish, smoke, github-release; build runs `python scripts/changelog.py release --tag "$GITHUB_REF_NAME"` (line 31) before `python -m build` (38) and uploads dist/; pypi-publish uses pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish in environment pypi with id-token (55-69); smoke loops attempts 1..6 with sleep 15 (98-113) and runs sqllens --version and validate (126-127); prerelease is `contains(version, '-')` (162). But the doc says 'Four jobs run in order' and lists smoke before github-release. In the workflow, smoke has `needs: [build, pypi-publish]` (76) and github-release has `needs: [build, pypi-publish]` (131). github-release does not depend on smoke, so the two run in parallel after publish. The doc's claim of a strict sequential order is therefore wrong for those two jobs.
